content:
Get help promptly

Giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, is inflammation of arteries that can threaten sight. If you think you may have it, ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111. Do not wait for a routine headache appointment. If you suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes, or have sudden severe eye pain, go to A&E or call 999. Do not drive yourself.

Symptoms to explain

Tell the clinician about a new or severe headache, tenderness at the temples or scalp, jaw pain when chewing or talking, and any change in vision. Tiredness, weight loss and flu-like symptoms can also occur. Symptoms overlap with other conditions, so this page cannot diagnose the cause.

Vision changes need urgent attention

Blurred or double vision, a dark shadow or other new visual changes need urgent GP or NHS 111 assessment. Tell them if these occur with headache, scalp tenderness or jaw pain. NHS temporal-arteritis guidance says people with vision problems should have a same-day hospital eye-specialist appointment. Sudden inability to see or sudden severe eye pain uses the emergency route above.

What assessment may involve

A clinician may examine you, arrange blood tests and refer you for specialist assessment. Ultrasound of the temporal arteries or a biopsy may be used. Because delayed treatment can risk sight, clinicians may begin steroid treatment before the diagnosis is fully confirmed.

Treatment and follow-up

Treatment commonly involves prednisolone with a plan to reduce it under supervision. Follow-up checks both the disease and treatment side effects. Do not suddenly stop prescribed steroids. Ask your team whom to contact if symptoms return or new vision symptoms appear.
